summary: The first in a planned series of surveys by Charles Kline at UCLA asking ARPANET sites how they had implemented host-to-host protocol. This one covers Network Control Programs, the software that handled network connections, and asks for a reply within two weeks. Later surveys were to cover Telnet and RJE.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 460 asks network sites to describe the software that manages their host-to-host connections. The answers were intended to show how the sites' Network Control Programs were built and operated.

subtitle: A questionnaire about how network sites built their Network Control Programs.

tldr.problem: The author wanted information about how different sites implemented the host-to-host protocol.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 460 defines what it calls an NCP and asks sites to answer questions about its hardware, code, buffers, protocol features, timeouts and network use.
tldr.outcome: Replies were requested within two weeks, and the results were to be published. The RFC says later surveys would cover Telnet, RJE and other topics.

today: The unit records RFC 460's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The document is a questionnaire about NCP implementations, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: What the Survey Covers
sections.content:
Charles Kline calls this the first in a series of requests for information about host-to-host protocol implementations. He asks all sites to reply within two weeks and says the results will be published. The survey concerns Network Control Programs (NCPs); later requests are expected to cover Telnet and remote job entry (RJE).

The RFC defines an NCP as the part of a system that performs the host-to-host protocol tasks described in the protocols notebook, NIC document 7104. It says an NCP may contain several kinds of code, even if they are not separate components.
sections.plainLanguage: This questionnaire asks sites how they implemented the software that handles host-to-host networking. The author planned to publish the answers and ask about other network services in later surveys.

sections.title: The Parts of an NCP
sections.content:
The author's model of an NCP includes code to establish connections and maintain a rendezvous table of open and pending connections. It also includes code for transmission on open connections, including buffer management and allocate and giveback commands.

Other parts move messages in and out of the Imp, sometimes using a separate processor or an Imp handler. The RFC also includes measurement, initialization and other code in its definition of an NCP.
sections.plainLanguage: An NCP sets up connections, moves messages, and manages the buffers used for network traffic. The survey treats these jobs as parts of one overall program, even when a site organizes them differently.

sections.title: Questions for Each Site
sections.content:
The questionnaire asks for the host name, site number, main computer and operating system, as well as information about documentation and the Imp interface. It asks who wrote and maintains the NCP, how much effort its development took, and the sizes of its code and tables.

Further questions cover communication between the NCP, Imp handler and user processes; supported byte sizes; buffer allocation and giveback; error handling; connection queuing; protocol experiments; timeouts; measurements of network effects; and planned changes. Respondents are told to mark items not applicable where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites are asked about the people, machines, code and memory behind their NCPs. They also describe how their systems handle traffic, errors, waiting connections and timeouts.
